A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same proto-token reconstruction study despite the title change from 'Latent' to 'Hidden'. All pages, equations, tables and figures are readable. Both end with references; neither supplied PDF contains appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction, token-arrangement, token-sharing, throughput and embedding-geometry experiments using six language models and four text sources.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds optimization-time measurements and a preliminary experiment using proto-tokens directly as autoregressive context.

M1.justification: Both optimize the same two embeddings, arrange inputs as one e followed by repeated m, and reconstruct text through a frozen model with causal attention. The explicit cross-entropy formula documents the existing objective. The new autoregressive probe tests the representations without changing the proposed reconstruction method.

E1.justification: The four text sources remain unchanged. v2 adds a limited test scenario using PG-19-derived representations directly as autoregressive context with proto-token/BOS combinations, testing access to encoded information beyond the prescribed one-pass reconstruction.

E2.justification: Both retain the autoregressive memory-token comparison under one- and two-trainable-embedding conditions. Newly cited speculative, multi-token and diffusion approaches are discussed but are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The new probe uses 50 PG-19 contexts of 128 tokens, generates 256-token continuations with Llama-3.2-1B, fits embeddings to their first 128 tokens, and visually assesses subsequent autoregressive outputs. v2 also evaluates optimization time across lengths. Existing reconstruction budgets, models and the 0.99 accuracy threshold remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a diagnostic experiment asking whether encoded information can be accessed by directly supplying proto-tokens as autoregressive context, plus an analysis of optimization time across sequence lengths. Existing arrangement, sharing, similarity and connectivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both retain ten-seed aggregation for token sharing, the same max/average reporting, and unchanged uncertainty displays in the retained tables and plots. v2 introduces no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or statistical tests for its additional evaluations.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain identical numerical values, and the reported 279-fold decoding throughput advantage remains unchanged. New Table 4 reports optimization times, including 215 seconds for Llama-3.1-8B at 512 tokens. The new autoregressive probe reports meaningless or unrelated outputs. Figure 1 summarizes existing capacity results rather than adding performance gains.

T1.justification: v1 Equation 3 and v2 Equation 4 define the same quadratic Bezier curve; the integral objective is rewritten as an equivalent expectation. The added loss formula restates existing cross-entropy training. Correcting 'degree-one' to 'degree-two' aligns the prose with the existing formula without changing the mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central reconstruction and embedding-geometry claims remain. However, v2's first contribution calls one token 'universal for all texts', stronger than v1's conclusion that it can in principle be shared across many texts. The revised conclusion explicitly frames the work as an existence demonstration and develops its prospective encoder-based applications.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the contextual-information effect as small with heavily overlapping distributions, concluding that representations mostly encode the target text. It adds the failure of direct autoregressive use as an applicability boundary and explicitly explains why incomplete optimization prevents precise capacity bounds and why practical use requires an encoder.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies Adam for Bezier control-point optimization and reports training times in Table 4. It removes v1's statement that reconstruction timing uses PyTorch profiling tools. The hardware and main hyperparameters remain unchanged, and the same code link is relocated to the introduction.

R1.justification: The introduction adds seven works covering speculative decoding, multi-token/blockwise prediction, and masked or diffusion generation, broadening the motivation around reusing pretrained models. The central positioning relative to memory-token compression and prompt tuning remains. Kuratov et al.'s publication update refers to the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, rewrites the opening motivation, clarifies the connectivity explanation, and revises portions of the conclusion and limitations. It standardizes p/m terminology and adds an embedding-space subheading and acknowledgments. The overall section structure and most experimental exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a capacity-summary Figure 1 and training-time Table 4. The original schematic moves into the method section as Figure 2; retained plots are relocated or renumbered, with caption and axis-label refinements. The two-column layout and structures of Tables 1–3 remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: Training-time Table 4, the negative direct-use experiment, and clearer qualifications about contextual information and capacity estimates improve transparency about practical costs and limitations. These are useful but limited gains over an unchanged core empirical foundation. The new probe remains qualitative, no practical encoder is demonstrated, and the stronger universal-sharing wording is not supported by additional sharing evidence.
